main.title: Phantasy Star IV: The End of the Millennium
main.subtitle: Science fiction told in illustrated panels
main.summary: Phantasy Star IV first appeared on Japan’s Mega Drive on December 17, 1993. Sega’s fourth numbered Phantasy Star returns to a science-fiction world living among the remains of an advanced civilisation. A young hunter, called Rudy in Japan and Chaz in the English version, begins his journey alongside the experienced Alys. What starts as work for hunters grows into a much larger conflict. Illustrated panels interrupt the exploration to frame conversations and dramatic moments, giving the story a visual rhythm closer to a comic than a succession of static text boxes.

cards.heading: Hunters among the ruins
cards.text: Phantasy Star IV first appeared on Japan’s Mega Drive on December 17, 1993. Sega’s fourth numbered Phantasy Star returns to a science-fiction world living among the remains of an advanced civilisation. A young hunter, called Rudy in Japan and Chaz in the English version, begins his journey alongside the experienced Alys. What starts as work for hunters grows into a much larger conflict. Illustrated panels interrupt the exploration to frame conversations and dramatic moments, giving the story a visual rhythm closer to a comic than a succession of static text boxes.

cards.heading: A party that fights together
cards.text: Travel, towns and encounters with front-facing enemies build on the series’ role-playing foundations, while combination attacks make the party’s cooperation tangible. Certain techniques can join into a stronger action when the right characters act in sequence; choosing commands is therefore also a question of coordination. The original manual devotes a section to this combination battle system. Music credited to Izuho Takeuchi, also known as Izuho Numata, and Masaki Nakagaki carries the journey between settlements, machinery and hostile landscapes.

main.title: Mega Man X
main.summary: Mega Man X is a 1993 platform game developed and published by Capcom for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.heading: X and Zero enter a new century
cards.text: Mega Man X is Capcom's 1993 Super NES action-platformer, beginning a new branch of the Mega Man series. A century after the earlier games, humans live alongside Reploids: robots capable of thought and feeling. X joins the Maverick Hunters, with Zero as his partner, to stop Sigma and the renegade robots threatening humanity. The new setting gives the familiar struggle between robots a different cast and a more distant future.

cards.heading: Dash, wall jumps and armor expand play
cards.text: With the transition to more advanced gaming hardware, series artist Keiji Inafune explained that the development of Mega Man X involved reinventing Mega Man through gameplay expansion and a more mature storyline while still maintaining the basic concepts on which the franchise was built. Much like the NES Mega Man games that came before it, Mega Man X is a platform game where the player takes control of the eponymous character and must complete a set of eight, initial stages in any order desired. Defeating the boss character at the end of each stage grants the player one new weapon that can then be toggled and used at will for the remainder of the game. However, Mega Man X adds a number of new features and makes radical changes to the original gameplay mechanics of previous releases in the series. These include allowing the player to dash along the ground, scale walls, and obtain armor attachments which grant special abilities.

cards.heading: Ports and rereleases sustain the first X
cards.text: Critics praised Mega Man X for its movement, graphics and sound, and it became a lasting Super NES success. The series continued with Mega Man X2 in 1994. The original later reached computers, mobile devices and several Nintendo download services, while PSP received the reworked Mega Man Maverick Hunter X. Collections and the Super NES Classic Edition brought it to further generations. These returns kept its opening adventure available alongside the sequels that developed its ideas.

main.title: Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden 2
main.summary: Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden 2 is a 1993 fighting video game developed by Tose and published by Bandai for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.text: Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden 2 is a 1993 fighting video game developed by Tose and published by Bandai for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System. Based upon Akira Toriyama's Dragon Ball franchise, it is the sequel to Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden, which was released earlier in 1993 for SNES. Following the Cell Games arc and a side-story about characters from the films Dragon Ball Z: Broly – The Legendary Super Saiyan and Dragon Ball Z: Bojack Unbound, its gameplay remains relatively the same as the original Super Butōden, consisting of one-on-one fights using a main six-button configuration, featuring special moves as well as three playable modes.

Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden 2 was developed by most of the same team who previously worked on the first Super Butōden entry shortly after its completion. The team wanted to increase the number of playable stages, implement adventure elements to the tournament mode, as well as feature characters from the Dragon Ball Z films in the project. Super Butōden 2 garnered positive reception from critics; most reviewers praised the presentation, visuals, audio, gameplay and improvements made over its predecessor but others regarded it to be similar to Super Butōden and felt mixed in regards to various design aspects. It was followed by Dragon Ball Z: Super Butōden 3 in 1994.

main.title: The Jungle Book
main.subtitle: The original Mega Drive journey, 1994
main.summary: The Jungle Book brought Mowgli’s journey to Mega Drive in 1994 under Virgin’s publishing label. This version’s original credits name both Virgin’s creative team and Eurocom, whose programmers and level designers helped turn the animated film into a scrolling platform adventure. Mowgli runs, jumps and climbs through the jungle towards the human village, encountering familiar figures such as Baloo, Bagheera and Shere Khan.

cards.heading: Finding a path through the jungle
cards.text: The Jungle Book brought Mowgli’s journey to Mega Drive in 1994 under Virgin’s publishing label. This version’s original credits name both Virgin’s creative team and Eurocom, whose programmers and level designers helped turn the animated film into a scrolling platform adventure. cards.heading: Gems before the journey can continue
cards.text: Progress requires exploration as well as reaching the end of a screen. Mowgli must collect the required gems before completing a chapter, with a compass pointing towards the nearest one and a time limit keeping him moving. Vines, trees and throwing weapons make the route more than a straight run to the right. The original manual credits the Sherman brothers for I Wanna Be Like You and Terry Gilkyson for The Bare Necessities, alongside the game’s own music team. The Mega Drive version later returned in the expanded Disney Classic Games Collection.

main.title: The Lion King
main.subtitle: Westwood’s original 1994 platform adventure
main.summary: The Lion King turned Simba’s journey from cub to adult into a platform game in 1994. Developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin, its original 16-bit versions brought the film’s landscapes and characters to Super Nintendo and Mega Drive. The Pride Lands, the elephant graveyard and the wildebeest stampede become places to cross rather than scenes to watch. The change in Simba’s age gives the adventure its structure: the player returns to familiar actions with a body that can now do more.

cards.heading: Growing into the jump
cards.text: The Lion King turned Simba’s journey from cub to adult into a platform game in 1994. Developed by Westwood Studios and published by Virgin, its original 16-bit versions brought the film’s landscapes and characters to Super Nintendo and Mega Drive. cards.heading: Two ages, two ways to fight
cards.text: Young Simba mainly survives by jumping on enemies and using a roar that must recharge. Adult Simba adds claw attacks and the ability to maul or throw opponents; grabbing ledges and moving through the environment remain central. The Mega Drive manual credits Matt Furniss of Krisalis for Genesis music and sound. Later collections reunited the original versions with modern viewing and save options.

main.title: Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3
main.subtitle: A fortune for Wario
main.summary: Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3 is Nintendo's 1994 Game Boy platform game starring Mario's rival. Wario travels to Captain Syrup's pirate island in search of enough treasure to pay for his own castle. His shoulder charge and changing hats give the familiar journey through platforms and blocks a heavier, more forceful character.

cards.heading: A fortune for Wario
cards.text: Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3 is Nintendo's 1994 Game Boy platform game starring Mario's rival. Wario travels to Captain Syrup's pirate island in search of enough treasure to pay for his own castle. His shoulder charge and changing hats give the familiar journey through platforms and blocks a heavier, more forceful character.

cards.heading: Putting his shoulder into it
cards.text: The shoulder charge sends Wario straight into enemies and breakable blocks. A stunned opponent can be picked up and thrown, turning one obstacle into a way to deal with another. Spikes still punish a careless approach. Reading which part of an enemy is exposed matters as much as committing to the charge, especially when a narrow platform leaves little room to stop.

cards.heading: A hat for another route
cards.text: Different hats change which routes Wario can attempt. Bull Wario breaks blocks with greater force and can cling to a ceiling by his horns. Jet Wario crosses a gap in a burst of flight, while Dragon Wario breathes fire. A power-up therefore changes more than the next fight: it can make a space above, below or beyond the current path worth another look.

cards.heading: Spending the treasure
cards.text: Coins have practical uses during the journey. Wario can turn ten into a single large coin to throw into a checkpoint or a locked exit, spending part of the wealth he came to collect. After a stage, a bonus game offers another gamble over the earnings. The promise of a castle keeps those small decisions connected to the reason he set out.

main.title: Virtua Fighter 2
main.summary: Virtua Fighter 2 is a 1994 fighting game developed and published by Sega for arcades.

cards.text: Virtua Fighter 2 is a 1994 fighting game developed and published by Sega for arcades. It is the second game in the Virtua Fighter series and the sequel to Virtua Fighter (1993). Created by Sega's Yu Suzuki-headed AM2 team, it was designed on the purpose-made Sega Model 2 hardware, which provided a significant upgrade in graphical capabilities. Following its release in arcades, Virtua Fighter 2 was ported to the Sega Saturn in November 1995, while ports for other platforms appeared later.

Virtua Fighter 2 was critically acclaimed for its gameplay and breakthrough graphics; it introduced the use of texture-mapped 3D characters, and was one of the first video games to use motion capture animation technology. It became a major arcade hit, selling more than 40,000 arcade units worldwide, and becoming one of Sega's best-selling arcade games of all time. The Saturn version was also well-received for its graphics and gameplay, becoming a blockbuster hit in Japan and selling relatively well in other markets, with more than 2 million units. The game was succeeded by Virtua Fighter 3 in 1996.

main.title: Daytona USA
main.summary: Daytona USA is a 1994 racing game developed by Sega AM2 and published by Sega for arcades.

cards.text: Daytona USA is a 1994 racing game developed by Sega AM2 and published by Sega for arcades. Inspired by the popularity of the NASCAR motor racing series in the United States, it has players race stock cars on one of three courses. It was the first game released on the Sega Model 2 arcade system board.

Sega partnered with GE Aerospace to develop the Model 2, which renders 3D graphics capable of texture filtering and texture mapping. Daytona USA was developed by AM2 after a meeting of the heads of Sega's regional offices to decide on a game to debut the Model 2 hardware. The concept was suggested by Tom Petit, president of Sega's American arcade division, with input from AM2 director Toshihiro Nagoshi, who became the game's director and producer. Sega aimed to outperform Namco's Ridge Racer (1993). The developers researched motorsports extensively; they mapped Daytona International Speedway, and their experience developing Virtua Racing (1992) helped with lighting and camera control.

Daytona USA became one of the highest-grossing arcade games of all time, and was a critical and commercial success, with its graphics, soundtrack and gameplay receiving high praise. The game was ported to the Sega Saturn in 1995, and was followed by sequels and enhanced versions for consoles and arcades. It has been frequently named one of the best video games.

main.title: Fire Emblem: Mystery of the Emblem
main.summary: Fire Emblem: Mystery of the Emblem, known in Japan as Fire Emblem: Monshō no Nazo, is a 1994 tactical role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Super Famicom.

cards.text: Fire Emblem: Mystery of the Emblem, known in Japan as Fire Emblem: Monshō no Nazo, is a 1994 tactical role-playing video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Super Famicom. It is the third installment of the Fire Emblem series, and the first to be developed for the Super Famicom. The story is divided into two parts: the first is a retelling of Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light, while the second is an original story acting as a sequel to the first game. After defeating the sorcerer Gharnef and the Dark Dragon Medeus, peace is restored to Archanea and Marth restores his kingdom. His ally Hardin ascends to the throne of Archanea, but begins hostile military expansion across the continent, forcing Marth to confront his old friend and the force driving him. Gameplay follows the traditional Fire Emblem system of tactical battles taking place on grid-based maps.

Mystery of the Emblem began development in 1992 during the production of Fire Emblem Gaiden. The staff from previous entries, including series creator Shouzou Kaga and composer Yuka Tsujiyoko, returned to their respective roles. While originally conceived as two separate projects, the team eventually merged the proposed remake of Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light with the original story content of Mystery of the Emblem. The gameplay returned to the formula of the original Fire Emblem game, which the more experimental Gaiden had veered away from in many regards. The difficulty was also lowered to encourage new players to try the series.

The game has been positively received by video game journalists; much praise went to its gameplay refinements and technical quality. It also set the best first-week sales for the series until Fire Emblem Awakening in 2012, and with 776,338 units by 2002 was the best-selling title in the series to that date. A derivative title for the Satellaview, BS Fire Emblem, was released during 1997. A full remake for the Nintendo DS, Fire Emblem: New Mystery of the Emblem, was released in 2010. In 2017, it was rereleased in Japan as part of the Japanese retailer versions of Classic SNES Edition.

main.title: Sonic the Hedgehog 3
main.summary: Sonic the Hedgehog 3 is a 1994 platform game developed by Sega Technical Institute and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis.

cards.text: Sonic the Hedgehog 3 is a 1994 platform game developed by Sega Technical Institute and published by Sega for the Sega Genesis. Like previous Sonic games, players traverse side-scrolling levels while collecting rings and defeating enemies. They control Sonic and Tails, who attempt to retrieve the Chaos Emeralds to stop Doctor Robotnik from relaunching his space station, the Death Egg, after it crash-lands on a mysterious floating island. Sonic 3 introduces Knuckles the Echidna, the island guardian, who lays traps for Sonic and Tails.

Development began in January 1993 by Sega Technical Institute in California, shortly after the release of Sonic the Hedgehog 2. It was initially developed as an isometric game, similar to what became Sonic 3D Blast (1996), but became a conventional 2D platformer due to time constraints. The pop musician Michael Jackson composed portions of the soundtrack but left the project and went uncredited; sources vary on how much of his work was retained, and many tracks were replaced in rereleases.

Sonic 3 was developed simultaneously with Sonic & Knuckles; they were planned as a single game until time constraints and cartridge costs forced the developers to split it. The Sonic 3 cartridge can be attached to an adapter on the Sonic & Knuckles cartridge, creating a combined game, Sonic the Hedgehog 3 & Knuckles.

Sonic 3 was released in North America and Europe in February 1994, and in Japan in May. As with its predecessors, it was a critical and commercial success, with critics seeing it as an improvement over previous installments. Sonic 3 and Sonic & Knuckles sold a combined four million copies worldwide, placing them among the bestselling Genesis games. They have been rereleased in various compilations.
